intended_object: The "successor constructor" of the terminal sequence 1, F1, F²1, …: the canonical map F(F^n 1) → F^{n+1} 1. I inferred this from the docstring, from the definitions of `Iter₀` and `Iter` just above it, and from how `project` and `unfold` use it.
explanation:
`Iter F n` is a wrapper structure around `(Iter₀ F n).Carrier`, which is F^n applied to the one-point space. Because of the wrapper, F(Iter F n) and Iter F (n+1) are not definitionally the same type. `succ` bridges them: it applies F to the unwrapping map `getHom` and then wraps the result with `mk`. Its partner `unsucc` goes the other way, and the lemmas `succ_unsucc` and `unsucc_succ` show the two are inverse.

In mathematics, F^{n+1}(1) is by definition F(F^n(1)), so this map is just the identity. It exists only because of how the Lean encoding is set up. As code it is correct: it is the canonical isomorphism, and it is a quasi-Borel morphism because `Functor.map` of a morphism is a morphism and `mk` is a morphism. But it is an implementation device, not a mathematical notion in its own right, and Mathlib has no counterpart for it.
